3D Factory · rendering

Phases 2–4: the environment, the materials, and the tracer

Phase 1 corrected how light becomes pixels. These three phases correct what the light is, what a material is, and what the offline renderer does with both.

31 Jul 2026 +4 new modules cad_app 323 tests cad_solid 136 tests every figure rendered by the code it documents

Nothing below is a mock-up. Every image on this page was produced by running the new modules — env.rs's sky, color.rs's transforms, matball.rs's BRDF, pathtrace.rs's tracer and denoiser — from a test that regenerates them on demand. If the code changes, the figures change with it.

Read this first

There is one thing to do before anything else: launch the app. Four new GLSL programs were added (sky, SSAO, blur, and a rewritten surface shader). Shader compilation cannot be tested without a GPU context, so the driver is the only real check. Compilation no longer crashes the app if it fails — see §2.6 — but if something is wrong you will see it, and the console will name the program.

§ 1How to see the changes

Everything new is reachable from two places. Nothing changes appearance until you turn daylight on, except the material library and the material ball, which are immediate.

☀ Sun / daylight → “Environment”

  1. Tick “Light the scene by the sun”. Until this is on, the viewport keeps the old fixed studio key light. Everything below is greyed out because it describes a sky, and without daylight there is no sky.
  2. Tick “Draw the sky behind the model”. The flat dark backdrop is replaced by the actual sky that is lighting the scene. This is the fastest way to confirm the whole environment path is alive — if the backdrop is a real graduated sky with a sun in it, the same function is feeding every surface.
  3. Drag Turbidity from 2 to 9. Watch the shadow side of the model, not the sky. At 2 the ambient is cold and blue and the contrast is hard; at 9 it goes white, flat and soft. That is the sky's colour genuinely reaching the surfaces, which a slider on a backdrop image could not do.
  4. Drag Reflections from 0 to 1 with a metal or a polished floor in view. At 0 a metal is black, because a metal has no diffuse — all it can do is reflect. At 1 it mirrors the sky.
  5. Toggle “Ambient occlusion”. Look at wall-to-floor junctions, under furniture, and inside cabinet carcasses. Then look at a surface in direct sunlight: it should barely change. That asymmetry is the design — see §2.4.
  6. Change the hour. The sky's colour, its gradient, the ambient on every surface, the shadows and the reflections now all move together, because they are one model.

🎨 Materials Factory

  1. Select any material. A rendered material ball now sits at the top of the right panel, under a fixed studio sky, showing roughness, metal, relief and the pattern at its real one-metre scale.
  2. Open the library and apply “Oak”, then “Chrome”, then “Copper”. The library was rebuilt on measured values — see §3.2.
  3. On a procedural, find the new “Surface” block: Rough A→B and Relief. Set Rough A→B to 0.72 and 0.48 on oak and rotate the view: the highlight now breaks along the grain instead of sliding over it as one sheet.
  4. “📂 Load PBR texture set…” — point it at any folder downloaded from ambientCG, Poly Haven or Quixel. It sorts base colour, normal, roughness, metallic and occlusion by filename and binds all of them at once.
  5. On an image material, tick “World-space (triplanar)” and set tiles/m. The texture now has a size in metres rather than one repeat per face.

⏺ Render

The denoise checkbox next to the samples slider. Start a CPU render at 8–16 samples and toggle it — see §4.3.

§ 2Phase 2 — the environment is a light source

2.1  What was wrong

The ambient term was two colours interpolated by the surface normal's up-component:

vec3 amb = mix(u_ground_col, u_sky_col, 0.5 + 0.5 * N.z);

That expression can only produce a vertical gradient. Every vertical surface in a building — which is to say every wall — received exactly the same ambient light regardless of which way it faced. A north wall and a south wall were identical. There was no sky to reflect, so a metal had nothing to be a metal about, and no amount of correcting the material could fix it.

2.2  The sky is now a real model

cad_app/src/env.rs implements the Preetham analytic daylight model (Preetham, Shirley & Smits, 1999) — the closed form that physical-sky implementations descend from. One function gives the radiance arriving from any direction, and that one function does three jobs: it is drawn as the backdrop, integrated into the diffuse ambient, and mirrored by glossy surfaces. They cannot disagree, because they are the same function.

What is physical here, and what is not

The shape and colour of the sky are the published model. The absolute level is deliberately not: it is scaled so that the irradiance on an up-facing surface equals exactly what the previous code produced. That preserves the daylight calibration that was tuned against Blender. This change alters how light is distributed over the sky, not how much of it there is.

2.3  Spherical harmonics: the ambient a surface actually receives

Integrating the sky over the hemisphere per fragment is not affordable. Instead the dome is projected once per frame onto 9 spherical-harmonic coefficients, pre-convolved with the clamped cosine lobe (Ramamoorthi & Hanrahan). Evaluating it is then about a dozen instructions, and the shader and the CPU shading path read the same nine numbers.

2.4  Environment reflection, and why it needed a split-sum

A rough surface reflects a wide cone of the environment, not a single ray. The textbook answer is a prefiltered cubemap mip chain plus a 2D lookup table. Both are avoided here:

  • The blurred environment is interpolated between the two limits a prefiltered chain would produce — the sharp mirror direction, and the cosine-lobe average about that direction, which the SH coefficients already store. No render target, no upload.
  • The BRDF integral uses Karis's analytic fit instead of a LUT texture — within about a percent over the whole roughness range, and it costs no texture unit or bind.

2.5  Ambient occlusion — and the mistake it would have been

Sky lighting on its own makes a render flatter, not rounder: every point receives the sky's full irradiance for its normal, whether it sits on an open wall or wedged in the corner behind a sofa. Screen-space occlusion supplies the information the per-normal ambient throws away.

The obvious implementation — compute AO, multiply it into the finished image — is wrong, and wrong in a way that looks atmospheric enough to survive review: it greys out a crease standing in full sunlight. Occlusion describes how much sky a point can see. It has nothing to say about the sun.

So the renderer now writes two light buffers:

Occlusion scales attachment 1 and nothing else. A corner in shadow darkens fully; the same corner in sunlight barely moves, because most of its light is in attachment 0. Two tests pin this — occlusion_only_scales_the_ambient_term checks the composite is literally c.rgb + a * ao and that no other shader samples the buffer, and every_geometry_pass_writes_both_render_targets catches a pass that forgot the second output (which leaves it undefined, i.e. garbage, and only for that pass).

The same split applies to the CPU-shaded flat geometry: each vertex now carries the ambient share of its baked colour, computed alongside the shade. Without it, AO on the flat path would have had to be a guess.

2.6  Shader compilation no longer kills the app

compile() used to panic!. That panic fires inside the egui paint callback, on the GL thread, at the first 3D frame — the window is already up, so the user sees the app die rather than a shader error, and every other feature dies with it. It now returns None, logs which program failed and why, and the feature that program drove simply stops drawing. With four new programs added in this phase, that was not optional.

Tests that can catch what a unit test normally cannot

GLSL cannot be compiled without a GPU context. So the shader tests check the failures that string substitution actually causes: a placeholder left unreplaced, a helper called before it is pasted in, a uniform the Rust side looks up by a name the source never declares (which silently yields None — “the slider does nothing”), a pass that writes only one of two render targets, and tone-mapping appearing anywhere but the composite.

§ 3Phase 3 — materials that behave like materials

3.1  One pattern, three channels

A real surface changes its finish wherever it changes its colour. Oak's dark early-wood is duller and physically lower than the pale late-wood beside it. Mortar is rougher than the tile it surrounds. Previously a procedural drove colour and nothing else, so every pattern was a picture printed on a sheet of uniform plastic.

The shader now evaluates the pattern field once and reads three things off it: the colour ramp, a roughness range (surf_rough), and a bump derived from the field's own gradient by central differences. One field, so they cannot come apart.

3.2  The library, rebuilt on measured values

Three things changed across all 33 presets.

WhatWhy it matteredExamples
Albedos from measured reflectance Too-bright albedos are why bounced light goes milky — every bounce multiplies the error. Architectural white paint measures ~0.78, not 0.90; fresh concrete ~0.35, not 0.50. Matte white 0.88 0.80 · Concrete 0.57 0.40 · Sandstone 0.76 0.68
Metals use their real F0 With metallic = 1, a metal's base colour is its Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence. That is a physical constant, not a taste decision. Copper 0.90,0.55,0.42 0.95,0.64,0.54 · Gold 1.00,0.78,0.34 1.00,0.77,0.34 · Chrome 0.95,0.96,0.97 · Brass added
Fake metals removed “Varnished oak” was metallic 0.22 and “Satin white” 0.12, faking a sheen. That tints the highlight with the surface's own colour, which is what a metal does and a varnished plank does not. Both are now dielectrics with a low roughness and an IOR — which is what a clearcoat is. Varnished oak → rough 0.14, ior 1.52 · Satin white → rough 0.22, ior 1.50
Every procedural varies its finish See §3.1. Concrete, sandstone, fabric and carpet also gained relief. Oak 0.72→0.48 · Concrete 0.94→0.80, bump 0.45 · Carpet 1.00→0.92, bump 0.9

3.3  The material ball

A flat swatch cannot show roughness, metal, IOR, relief, or what the sky puts back into a glossy surface. Those are only legible on a curved surface with an environment behind it. The preview is rendered on the CPU with the same maths as the viewport — which makes it a standing cross-check: if the ball and the viewport ever disagree, something between them is wrong. A test (the_preview_agrees_with_the_viewports_brdf) reads the GLSL back out of light3d.rs and asserts the pieces that would silently drift are still spelled the same way over there, including the π factor that carries the app's entire sun calibration.

The sphere is one metre across, at the world origin. That matters: procedurals are evaluated in world space, so the ball shows the pattern at the size it would appear on a one-metre object. A preview that quietly rescaled the pattern to fit would be the most misleading thing it could do.

3.4  PBR texture sets, from a folder

Every free texture library ships the same thing: five or six maps in one folder, distinguished only by a suffix. Until now the app could take exactly one image, pasted from the clipboard, and used it as albedo — which is why an imported brick read as wallpaper. A brick wall with no normal map is flat, and with no roughness map it is uniformly shiny.

texture_set.rs classifies filenames and load_folder follows the classification. The subtleties are all in the ordering, and each one is a real bug avoided:

RuleWhat goes wrong without it
NormalDX tested before Normal Every DirectX map loads as OpenGL and every bump is lit from the wrong side. The material still renders and still looks like a material — it reads as “the lighting is a bit odd”, not as a bug. The green channel is inverted on load instead.
ao matched as a whole token As a substring it fires on any filename containing “ao”. A file called chao.png becomes an occlusion map.
Roughness before Gloss Some sets ship both. Glossiness is inverted into roughness on load, so exactly one convention exists downstream.
Height/Displacement before the generic greyscale names Both are greyscale; “Disp” vs “Rough” is the only tell. Relief loaded as gloss.
ARM/ORM unpacked into three maps Poly Haven ships occlusion, roughness and metalness packed into R, G and B of one image. Bound whole it would be read as a single greyscale map — wrong three ways at once. A dedicated file for any of the three still wins over the packed channel.
Only base colour uploads as sRGB Decoding a normal map through a display curve bends every normal toward the surface.

The tests use filenames copied from real downloads, not invented ones — a hand-made test set would agree with the code and prove nothing.

3.5  World-space (triplanar) mapping

Architecture here is CSG extruded from a 2D plan. It has no UVs worth the name — a wall promoted from a polyline has none at all — so “one image per face” was the only thing UV mapping could do with it. Triplanar projects the image on the three world axes and blends by the surface normal, at a fixed tiles per metre. A brick texture then has a physical size: set 2.0 and you get a 0.5 m tile, on any surface it lands on, at any angle, with no seams to author.

§ 4Phase 4 — the path tracer

4.1  It was not sampling a BRDF

The bounce was: reflect about the mirror direction, then lerp toward a cosine lobe by roughness². That is not a BRDF. It has no Fresnel, it is not normalised, and it converges to the wrong image no matter how many samples you give it — so more samples made a cleaner picture of the wrong answer.

It is now the same Cook-Torrance GGX the viewport runs, with proper importance sampling: a half-vector drawn from D(h)·(n·h), the estimator collapsing to 4·F·Vis·(n·l)·(v·h)/(n·h), and a lobe choice weighted by how much light each lobe is likely to carry, divided back out to stay unbiased.

The furnace test

A wrong importance-sampling weight still produces a picture, still converges, and converges to the wrong brightness. The only way to catch it is a white furnace test: put a white surface in a uniform environment of radiance L and check that L comes back. a_white_surface_in_a_uniform_furnace_returns_what_it_receives does this at four roughness/metallic combinations. The tolerances are honest about the model's own limits — single-scattering GGX loses energy at high roughness (no multiple scattering between microfacets) and dielectrics gain a little (the diffuse is not reduced by the Fresnel that was reflected). Both are shared with the viewport, and both are far smaller than the errors a sampling mistake makes.

Why there is no MIS weight

The sun is sampled explicitly at every bounce. A scattered ray that also saw the sun's disc would count the same light twice — so the disc is included only for rays that reach the camera without scattering. That is the standard treatment of a delta light: next-event estimation handles it, BSDF sampling excludes it, and no multiple-importance weight is needed anywhere. Adding one would have been the wrong answer to a problem that does not exist here.

Next-event estimation also gained the specular lobe. It previously multiplied by albedo alone, so a sun highlight on a polished floor was present in the viewport and completely absent from the render.

4.2  Procedurals reach the renderer

Procedurals existed only as GLSL, so the tracer could not see them: it was handed the ramp's midpoint colour and an oak cabinet rendered as one flat brown while the viewport showed the grain. proc_tex.rs is the Rust twin of the shader's evaluation, and both the tracer and the material ball read it.

The subtle one

GLSL's fract returns the positive fractional part; Rust's fract() keeps the sign of its input. Transcribing the noise hash without noticing puts a visible seam at the origin — on most walls, since a plan is drawn wherever the user drew it. Pinned by the_noise_lattice_survives_negative_coordinates.

4.3  The denoiser

Edge-aware à-trous wavelet filtering (Dammertz et al., 2010): five passes of a 5×5 B-spline kernel with the step doubling each time, reaching a 65-pixel neighbourhood at the cost of five 25-tap passes rather than one 4225-tap one. Each tap is weighted by how similar its colour, normal and depth are to the centre.

Two details do most of the work:

  • Albedo demodulation. The noise is in the lighting, not in the material. Dividing the albedo out before filtering and multiplying it back after lets the filter be wide enough to actually clean the light while the texture — which was never filtered — comes back untouched.
  • Firefly rejection first. A single path that found the sun through a near-mirror lobe lands one pixel hundreds of times brighter than its neighbours. The colour edge-stop then reads it as a genuine feature and protects it — so the one artefact the filter cannot remove is the one it is most needed for. Clamping each pixel into its own 3×3 neighbourhood first removes it before the edge test ever sees it, and costs nothing on well-sampled pixels.

A test builds two constant regions at very different depths with noise on top and asserts both halves: the noise falls by more than 60%, the mean survives, and the step across the silhouette is still there. A filter that only did the first is a smear.

§ 5Two things I fixed that were not in the plan

5.1  A double tone-map left over from Phase 1

Phase 1 moved the display transform to the composite and removed 1 − e⁻ˣ from the textured shader. It did not remove it from the CPU shading path in factory.rs, which bakes light into vertex colours for all flat-shaded geometry. So every flat-shaded surface under daylight was being tone-mapped twice — exactly the mistake Phase 1 existed to remove, just on the other path.

The CPU path now decodes the material's authored sRGB, multiplies by linear irradiance, and stops. The light stays scene-referred all the way to the composite. the_flat_path_stays_linear_and_untonemapped pins it by checking that four times the light gives four times the value.

5.2  Emissive materials did not emit

emission reached the path tracer but never the raster shader, so an emissive material glowed in a render and was inert in the viewport. It is now a uniform on the textured program, pre-multiplied by strength and decoded to linear, added to the direct buffer so occlusion cannot eat it.

§ 6What is not verified, and what I would watch

Unverified

None of the GLSL has been compiled by a driver. There is no GL context in a unit test. Four new programs and a substantially rewritten surface shader are in this change. The tests cover the failure modes string assembly causes, and a failure is now survivable rather than fatal, but the driver is the real check.

  • SSAO cost. 16 taps plus a 4×4 blur at full resolution, every frame. On a large scene this is the most expensive thing added. If it costs too much, the toggle is in the Sun dialog; halving the AO buffer's resolution would be the next step.
  • Procedural bump cost. Relief evaluates the noise field three extra times per fragment. It is off (0.0) unless a material asks for it, but the rebuilt library asks for it on wood, concrete, sandstone, plaster, fabric and carpet.
  • Triplanar cost. Three texture fetches per map instead of one, on materials that enable it.
  • The sky's SH bake runs 1024 sky evaluations per frame. Measured at well under a millisecond, but it is per-frame work that could be cached against the sun settings if it ever shows up in a profile.
  • The GPU path tracer is unchanged. It still runs the older two-colour environment in its own fragment shader. The CPU tracer got all of Phase 4. They will not match on a sky-heavy scene until the GPU backend is brought across.

Backward compatibility

An existing project loads unchanged. surf_rough defaults to an equal pair, which the renderer reads as “this pattern does not vary its finish, use the material's own roughness” — the previous behaviour exactly. bump defaults to 0. Daylight is still off by default, so the sky, the SH ambient and the sky reflections do nothing until it is switched on. The only unconditional visual changes are ambient occlusion (on by default, and it only touches ambient light) and the rebuilt library.
